analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every American affordable private health coverage, ending employer-based insurance and subsidizing premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in January 2007 with 17 cosponsors, including 10 Republicans, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee without any action until that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every adult to buy a standardized private health plan sold through a state 'Health Help Agency,' with subsidies for people up to four times the poverty line. It would have ended employer-sponsored coverage, the federal employees' health program, and children's SCHIP coverage, replacing them with the guaranteed private plans. Insurers would have to sell to everyone at community-rated premiums, meaning no price differences based on health status, age, or gender.
analysis.who_benefits: People without coverage and people priced out or denied coverage because of health conditions gain the most: every adult gets a guaranteed offer of a standardized private plan, premiums cannot be set based on health status, age, gender, or industry, and premium subsidies phase down from full coverage at the poverty line to partial help up to 400% of poverty. Children in families below 300% of poverty get coverage, plus school-based health centers. People in Medicare gain chronic-disease management and a requirement that the government negotiate Medicare drug prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Every adult is guaranteed the opportunity to buy a private plan with benefits at least equal to the standard federal employee Blue Cross/Blue Shield plan, including annual physicals and preventive care with no cost-sharing

Premiums must use adjusted community rating: insurers may not set rates based on age, gender, industry, health status, or claims experience, and subsidies cover the full premium for people at or below the poverty line, phasing out at 400% of poverty
Children in families below 300% of the poverty line are covered, school-based health centers are expanded with grants, and states get new flexibility for home- and community-based long-term care
Medicare is required to negotiate prescription drug prices directly, and the bill ends the tax deduction for direct-to-consumer prescription drug advertising

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who previously got 'free' employer coverage would pay a premium, sliding by income, plus cost-sharing ('personal responsibility contributions') on non-preventive care; people who stay uninsured face a late-enrollment penalty of the missed premiums plus 15%. Employers owe shared-responsibility payments, and the financing depends on redirecting Medicare and Medicaid funds (including 90% of Medicaid disproportionate-share hospital payments) and phasing out the employer health tax exclusion. Federal employees and SCHIP children lose their current programs and move into the new plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Premium-payers, employers, and public health programs

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a mandate with real penalties: adults who go 63 days without coverage owe back premiums plus 15%, those premiums are not dischargeable in bankruptcy, and nonpayment can affect an immigrant's status
Preexisting-condition protections are only 'similar' to the weaker rules in law at the time, not a full ban on preexisting-condition exclusions, so some new enrollees could still face waiting periods

It terminates SCHIP and folds children into private plans (with a Medicaid supplemental wrap), and requires Medicare Part B premiums to be adjustable based on 'healthy behaviors' — a design that shifts costs toward people who do not participate
The financing — converting employer health spending and recapturing Medicare and Medicaid funds into a new trust fund — was untested, and critics could not verify the math before the bill moved

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and concrete: guaranteed coverage, income-based subsidies, community-rated premiums that end health-status pricing, and Medicare drug-price negotiation. The costs are also real: a mandate with penalties, new premiums for people who previously had employer coverage at no charge, the dismantling of familiar programs like federal employee coverage and SCHIP, and financing that relied on redirecting Medicare and Medicaid money. The design deliberately routes the entire population through private insurers rather than a public plan, which guarantees universal coverage but also locks private insurance into the center of the system permanently.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Healthy Americans Act on January 18, 2007; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance
It attracted 17 cosponsors — 10 Republicans, 6 Democrats, and 1 Independent — an unusually bipartisan lineup for a universal-coverage bill
Wyden gave introductory remarks on the floor repeatedly through September 2007, but the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee with no floor action in either chamber

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system's participants kept what they had: employers kept the current tax exclusion and benefits role, insurers kept the employer-based market, and Medicare/SCHIP kept their existing structures. The uninsured and people facing health-status pricing gained nothing from the two years the bill sat without action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo and its participants

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 18, 2007 and delivered introductory floor remarks repeatedly through September 2007 to keep it visible

for.name: 10 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making universal coverage legislation bipartisan at the start of the 110th Congress

against.name: Senate Finance Committee

against.what_they_did: Took up the bill on referral but never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list split 10 Republicans, 6 Democrats, and 1 Independent, but the committee that controlled the bill's fate never brought it up, so no vote ever revealed how the chamber as a whole would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have made private insurers the permanent, mandatory channel for nearly all health coverage — every adult required to buy a plan — while imposing community rating, guaranteed issue, and standardized benefits on them. Universal coverage and the insurers' captive customer base would arrive together, by design.

Employers would stop providing and administering health coverage and instead owe shared-responsibility payments, losing the tax exclusion but gaining predictability. Workers who had employer coverage 'free' would see premiums come out in the open.
Medicare would be required to negotiate drug prices directly, and the tax deduction for direct-to-consumer prescription drug advertising would be disallowed — both cutting into drug industry revenue.
